title: Filter rows, then filter groups
why: WHERE runs before grouping and sees individual rows; HAVING runs after and sees aggregates. Put an aggregate in WHERE and the query is rejected; put a row condition in HAVING and you get a slower query that happens to work. Drill both halves in one statement until the order of operations is muscle memory rather than trial and error.

variations.prompt: Considering only order lines with a qty of 2 or more, count the lines per product and keep products with at least twenty of them: product_id and bulk_lines, ordered by bulk_lines descending then product_id ascending. The qty condition filters rows, the line count filters groups.
variations.reference: SELECT product_id, count(*)::BIGINT AS bulk_lines FROM order_items WHERE qty >= 2 GROUP BY product_id HAVING count(*) >= 20 ORDER BY bulk_lines DESC, product_id ASC

variations.prompt: For orders that are not cancelled, total the succeeded payment amounts per order status: status and revenue as DECIMAL(18,2), keeping only statuses whose total exceeds 1000. Order by status ascending.
variations.reference: SELECT o.status, sum(p.amount)::DECIMAL(18,2) AS revenue FROM orders o JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.order_id AND p.status = 'succeeded' WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled' GROUP BY o.status HAVING sum(p.amount) > 1000 ORDER BY o.status

variations.prompt: Count active products per category, keeping only categories with at least seven: category_id and active_products, ordered by category_id ascending. Filter the rows in WHERE, not the groups.
variations.reference: SELECT category_id, count(*)::BIGINT AS active_products FROM products WHERE active GROUP BY category_id HAVING count(*) >= 7 ORDER BY category_id
